transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: A new study has found that eating a handful of nuts every day can reduce the risk of heart disease by up to 20 percent, according to researchers at Harvard University. The study, which followed over 200,000 people for more than 30 years, found that people who ate nuts regularly—about one ounce or 28 grams per day—had significantly lower rates of heart disease, stroke, and premature death compared to people who rarely or never ate nuts. Researchers say that nuts are rich in healthy fats, fiber, vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants, all of which are good for heart health. Different types of nuts—including almonds, walnuts, peanuts, and cashews—all showed similar benefits, so it doesn't matter which kind you eat. However, researchers caution that nuts are also high in calories, so people should eat them in moderation and not add them to an already unhealthy diet. They recommend replacing less healthy snacks like chips or cookies with nuts instead of just adding nuts to your diet. The findings add to a growing body of evidence that nuts are an important part of a healthy diet.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: The city of Barcelona has introduced a new "superblock" system that transforms entire neighborhoods by closing off streets to car traffic and turning them into pedestrian-friendly spaces with parks, playgrounds, and outdoor seating. The superblock concept, which was first tested in Barcelona several years ago, involves grouping several city blocks together and restricting through traffic to only the main roads around the perimeter, while the streets inside the superblock are open only to pedestrians, bicycles, and local residents who need access to their homes. The result is quieter, cleaner, safer streets where children can play, neighbors can socialize, and people can walk and bike without worrying about cars. The city plans to create over 500 superblocks by 2030, covering nearly 25 percent of the city's streets. Early results from existing superblocks show significant reductions in air pollution and noise, as well as increased physical activity among residents. The idea has become so popular that other cities around the world, including Paris, New York, and Seoul, are now considering similar programs.
Questions 3 to 5 are based on the news report you have just heard.
3. What is a "superblock" in Barcelona?
4. What is one benefit of the superblock system mentioned?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Scientists at NASA have discovered a new planet outside our solar system that is remarkably similar to Earth in size and temperature, raising the possibility that it could potentially support life. The planet, named Kepler-452b, is located about 1,400 light-years away in the constellation Cygnus. It is only about 60 percent larger than Earth, and it orbits a star that is very similar to our sun, at roughly the same distance that Earth orbits the sun. This means that the planet receives a similar amount of light and heat from its star as Earth does, putting it in the so-called "habitable zone" where liquid water could exist on the surface. Scientists caution that they don't yet know if the planet has an atmosphere or water, or if it is actually habitable—more research is needed to determine its composition and conditions. But the discovery is exciting because it is the most Earth-like planet ever found orbiting a sun-like star. The discovery was made using data from NASA's Kepler space telescope, which has found thousands of exoplanets—planets orbiting other stars—since it was launched in 2009.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Hannah): Hey Tom, how was your winter break? Did you do anything fun?
Man (Tom): It was great! I went skiing in the French Alps with my family. It was amazing—we had perfect weather and the snow was great.
Woman: Wow, that sounds incredible! I've always wanted to try skiing, but I've never been. I'm kind of scared of falling and hurting myself, honestly.

Man: Oh, you should definitely try it! It's so much fun, and it's not as hard or as dangerous as you might think. You just have to start slow and take lessons first. I started taking lessons when I was a kid, and I still remember the first time I stood up on skis—I fell over immediately, but it was fun anyway.
Woman: Really? You think a total beginner like me could do it? I'm not very athletic, and I'm terrible at sports.

Man: Of course you could! Everyone starts as a beginner. And you don't have to be super athletic—skiing is more about technique and balance than strength. The first few days are just learning how to stop and turn and get used to the feeling of sliding on snow. You fall a lot at first, but that's part of the learning process, and the snow is soft so it doesn't hurt that bad.
Woman: Hmm, maybe. But isn't it expensive? I've heard ski trips are really costly—lift tickets, equipment rental, lessons, accommodation... It all adds up.

Man: It can be expensive, yeah, but there are ways to do it cheaper. Like, you can go during the week instead of weekends when prices are lower, or go to smaller, less famous resorts that aren't as expensive. And you don't need to buy all the gear at first—you can rent everything when you get there.
Woman: That's good to know. What about the cold? I hate being cold. I can barely handle winter here, and the Alps sound freezing.

Man: It is cold, but if you have the right clothes, you stay warm. You need a good waterproof jacket and pants, warm layers underneath, gloves, a hat, and goggles. And you're moving around a lot when you ski, so you actually work up a sweat sometimes. I often take my jacket off when I'm skiing because I get too warm.
Woman: Really? I wouldn't have expected that. So... do you think I should try it?

Man: Absolutely! I think you'd love it. It's such a fun way to be outside in the winter, and the views from the top of the mountain are absolutely breathtaking. There's nothing like skiing down a mountain with the sun shining and fresh snow all around you.

Woman: Hmm, you're making it sound really appealing. Maybe I should look into taking a lesson at the indoor ski slope near my city first, just to see if I like it before I spend money on a whole trip.

Man: That's a great idea! Indoor slopes are perfect for beginners—you can learn the basics in a controlled environment without having to travel all the way to the mountains. And if you decide you like it, then you can plan a real trip.
Woman: Yeah, that makes sense. Thanks for all the advice, Tom. You've almost convinced me to try it.
Man: No problem! Let me know if you do try it—I'd be happy to give you more tips or even come with you sometime.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Kevin): Hey Sarah, I heard you're studying abroad in Italy next semester. That's so exciting! Are you excited?

Woman (Sarah): I am excited, but I'm also really nervous. I've never been to another country before, and my Italian is not very good. What if I can't communicate with anyone? What if I get lost? What if I don't make any friends?

Man: Oh, don't worry so much! You'll be fine. I studied abroad in Spain two years ago, and I was nervous too, but it ended up being the best experience of my life. You learn so much more than just what's in the classroom.
Woman: Really? What was the hardest part for you at first?

Man: Oh, definitely the language barrier. Even though I had studied Spanish for three years, actually using it in real life was way harder than I expected. People talk fast, they use slang, and sometimes I couldn't understand anything at all. It was frustrating at first, but it gets better surprisingly fast. After a month or two, I was having conversations without even thinking about it.
Woman: That's encouraging. But I'm worried about making friends. I'm kind of shy, and it's hard for me to meet new people.

Man: I get that. But study abroad programs are perfect for meeting people because everyone is in the same boat—they're all new, they don't know anyone, and they want to make friends. There are usually orientation events and group trips at the beginning that help you meet people. And if you live with a host family or in a dorm with other international students, you automatically have people to hang out with.
Woman: I'm living with a host family, actually. I'm kind of nervous about that too. What if we don't get along? What if they're weird?

Man: Living with a host family was my favorite part of the whole experience! My host family was so nice, and they really made me feel at home. I learned so much about the culture from them—way more than I would have just from classes or traveling. And my Spanish improved so much faster because I had to speak it every day at dinner and around the house. Yeah, it can be awkward at first, but most host families are used to having international students and they know how to make you feel welcome.
Woman: That's good to hear. What about food? I'm a really picky eater. What if I don't like Italian food?

Man: Oh, come on—who doesn't like Italian food? Pizza, pasta, gelato... It's amazing. But seriously, even if you're picky, you'll find something you like. And part of the experience is trying new things. I tried all kinds of food in Spain that I never would have tried at home, and I ended up loving most of it.
Woman: I guess you're right. I'm probably overthinking this. It will be an adventure, right?
Man: Exactly! It's okay to be nervous—that's normal. But I promise you, you're going to have an amazing time. And you'll grow so much as a person from the experience.
Woman: Thanks, Kevin. That makes me feel better. I'm still nervous, but I'm also more excited now.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: The history of the Internet is a story of innovation, collaboration, and unexpected connections that transformed the world in ways no one could have predicted. What began as a small military research project in the 1960s has grown into a global network that connects billions of people and shapes nearly every aspect of modern life.

The origins of the Internet date back to the Cold War era, when the U.S. Department of Defense wanted to create a communication network that could survive a nuclear attack. The idea was that if part of the network was destroyed, information could still travel through the remaining parts, taking a different route to its destination. This project, called ARPANET, connected computers at universities and research institutions, and the first message was sent in 1969 between UCLA and Stanford University in California.

In the 1970s and 1980s, the network grew as more universities and research institutions joined, and new technologies were developed that allowed different networks to connect to each other, creating a "network of networks" that became known as the Internet. However, the Internet was still mostly used by researchers, scientists, and government agencies—it wasn't accessible to the general public.

That changed in the early 1990s with the invention of the World Wide Web by British scientist Tim Berners-Lee. The Web made the Internet much easier to use, with graphical web pages that could include text, images, and links that you could click on to go to other pages. Before the Web, you had to use complicated text-based commands to access information on the Internet. The first web browser, Mosaic, was released in 1993, and suddenly anyone with a computer could browse the Web easily.

Since then, the Internet has grown exponentially. In 1995, there were only about 16 million Internet users worldwide. Today, there are over 5 billion users—more than 60 percent of the world's population. The Internet has transformed how we communicate, work, learn, shop, entertain ourselves, and interact with the world. Social media, e-commerce, streaming video, online education, and smartphones have all been made possible by the Internet.

Of course, the Internet has also brought challenges—issues like privacy, misinformation, cybercrime, and digital divides between those who have access and those who don't. But there's no denying that the Internet has changed the world in profound ways, and its story is far from over.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: Music has been a part of human culture for thousands of years, and it exists in every society on Earth. But why do humans make music? And what effect does it have on us? Scientists and philosophers have been asking these questions for centuries, and while we still don't have all the answers, research has revealed some fascinating ways that music affects our brains, our bodies, and our emotions.

One of the most obvious effects of music is on our emotions. We all have experience with this—a sad song can make us cry, an upbeat song can make us feel happy and energetic, and a calm song can help us relax. But why does music have this power? Studies using brain imaging have found that listening to music activates the reward centers in our brain, releasing dopamine, the same chemical that's released when we eat good food, have sex, or take certain drugs. This is why music can feel so pleasurable and why we often seek it out when we want to change our mood.

Music also has surprising physical effects on the body. Slow, calming music can lower heart rate, blood pressure, and stress hormone levels, which is why music therapy is used to help patients recover from surgery, manage chronic pain, and reduce anxiety. On the other hand, fast, loud music can increase heart rate and adrenaline levels, which is why people listen to energetic music when they exercise or need to stay awake and alert.

Interestingly, research has found that playing music—actually learning an instrument and making music yourself—has even more benefits than just listening. Learning to play an instrument improves memory, attention, coordination, and problem-solving skills, and it can even increase IQ and academic performance in children. This is because playing music uses many different parts of the brain at once—the auditory cortex for hearing, the motor cortex for moving your fingers and hands, the frontal lobes for planning and attention, and the emotional centers for feeling and expressing the music.

Music also plays an important social role. Making music together—singing in a choir, playing in a band, or even just dancing together at a party—creates feelings of connection and bonding between people. This may be one of the reasons music evolved in the first place: it helped early humans form stronger social groups and work together more effectively.

While we may never fully understand why music has such powerful effects on us, there's no doubt that it enriches our lives in countless ways. Whether we're listening to it, playing it, or making it together, music is a fundamental part of what it means to be human.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: The United Nations has declared access to clean water a fundamental human right, yet billions of people around the world still lack access to safe drinking water and adequate sanitation. The water crisis is one of the most pressing global challenges of our time, affecting health, education, economic development, and gender equality.

The numbers are staggering. According to the World Health Organization, approximately 2 billion people worldwide do not have access to safely managed drinking water, and nearly half of the global population lacks access to safely managed sanitation services. Every year, millions of people die from diseases caused by unsafe water and poor sanitation, including diarrhea, cholera, and typhoid. Children are especially affected—water-related diseases are a leading cause of death for children under five years old.

The causes of the water crisis are complex and interconnected. Population growth and urbanization are increasing demand for water, while climate change is making water supplies more unpredictable, with more frequent droughts and floods. Pollution from agriculture, industry, and human waste is contaminating water sources, making them unsafe to drink. In many low-income countries, infrastructure for water treatment and distribution is inadequate or non-existent, forcing people to rely on unsafe water sources like rivers, ponds, or unprotected wells.

The water crisis also has a disproportionate impact on women and girls. In many parts of the world, it's the responsibility of women and girls to collect water for their families, which can mean walking several kilometers every day to the nearest water source. This takes time that could be spent going to school, working, or resting, and it can also be dangerous, as women and girls may face harassment or violence while traveling to collect water. When girls have to spend hours every day fetching water, they are less likely to attend school, which limits their opportunities and perpetuates cycles of poverty.

There are solutions, however. Technological innovations like low-cost water filters, solar-powered water pumps, and rainwater harvesting systems can help provide clean water to communities that lack infrastructure. Improving sanitation facilities and promoting good hygiene practices like handwashing can prevent many water-related diseases. Protecting watersheds and using water more efficiently in agriculture and industry can help ensure that there's enough clean water for everyone.

Addressing the water crisis requires cooperation between governments, organizations, communities, and individuals. It's not just a problem for developing countries—even wealthy nations face challenges with water scarcity, pollution, and aging infrastructure. Water is essential for all life, and ensuring that everyone has access to clean, safe water is one of the most important challenges we face as a global community.
